449.title: The city of nine gates
449.hook: King Puranjana moves into a city of nine gates and forgets his oldest friend: avidya, the wrong knowing at the root
449.carry: avidya: taking what passes for what lasts
449.tomorrow: the gods win a war and say, we did this. then fire can't burn one blade of grass.
449.howItsDone: Narada's story of King Puranjana, in the fourth book of the Bhagavata Purana, is read in Hindu teaching as a map of the self in the body, and Narada explains it himself. In yoga and Vedanta, avidya is treated as the root problem, and students practice discernment, noticing what passes and what remains, as the way to loosen it.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha's wonder. Five afflictions, one root: seeing wrongly. Today, that root up close.
screen: `FIVE AFFLICTIONS, ONE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Narada tells this one in the Bhagavata Purana. King Puranjana has an old friend who goes everywhere with him, a friend so quiet he is called only the unknown one. But the king is restless. He wanders the world until he finds a perfect city with nine gates, and a beautiful queen inside. He moves in, marries her, and the friend slips out of his mind. Then an army arrives at the gates, one the king never planned for.
screen: `A KING AND A QUIET FRIEND.` → `A CITY OF NINE GATES.` → `THE FRIEND, FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: The army belongs to a king called Chandavega, and his three hundred and sixty soldiers, some light and some dark, wear the city down. All those years Puranjana laughed when the queen laughed and wept when she wept, as if her every mood were his. Now the city burns, and he can't imagine himself without it. In his next life, his old friend finds him grieving and asks: don't you remember me? Then Narada gives the key. The city of nine gates is the body. The queen is the mind. The soldiers are the days and nights. Puranjana is you. And the friend you forgot is the Lord within. This is the Hindu teaching of avidya, ignorance, and Patanjali defines it in sutra 2.5 as four mix-ups: the passing taken as permanent, the impure as pure, what brings pain as pleasant, and the not-self as the self. The deepest is the last: taking the body, the moods, the roles for the self, when the self is the one living in them. Sutra 2.4 calls avidya the field, the soil the other afflictions grow in. It isn't a gap in your facts; everyone knows cities fall. Vidya is knowledge; avidya is its opposite, a wrong knowing that feels true from the inside. The commentator Vyasa compares it to an enemy, not just a missing friend. Today it looks ordinary: the friend group you assume will always be this close, a bad mood that feels like who you are. Not a reason for gloom. The friend never left. It's a reason to stop and remember.
screen: `AN ARMY AT THE NINE GATES.` · `'DON'T YOU REMEMBER ME?'` · `THE FORGOTTEN FRIEND: THE LORD WITHIN.` · `2.5: FOUR MIX-UPS.` · `THE FIELD THE OTHERS GROW IN.` · then, large: `THE PASSING, TAKEN AS LASTING.`

segments.voice: Notice something in you that feels permanent right now, a mood, a worry, a sense of who you are today, and ask it the question Puranjana forgot to ask: has this always been here, and will it always be? Watch it for a few breaths and see whether it shifts. Then notice what has been watching it the whole time, and rest there. If you pray, let that be a quiet hello to the friend within.
Ignorance. Avidya: not a lack of facts but a wrong knowing, taking the passing for the permanent, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self for the self.

450.title: Fire and the blade of grass
450.hook: the gods say a victory is theirs, and fire can't burn one blade of grass: asmita, the seer mistaken for its instruments
450.carry: asmita: the seer mistaken for what it sees
450.tomorrow: a king gives up a whole kingdom. can a baby deer undo him?
450.howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad's story of the gods and the blade of grass is a well-loved teaching about where power really comes from. In classical yoga, asmita is loosened through discernment between the seer and the seen; teachers often have students notice the difference between awareness and the thoughts and roles it is aware of, and many Hindus credit a success to God's grace before their own effort.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the greatest wonder, and your line, avidya: taking what passes for what lasts, ignorance at the root. Today, what grows first from that soil: the sense of me.
screen: `AVIDYA: TAKING WHAT PASSES FOR WHAT LASTS.`

segments.voice: The Kena Upanishad tells a story about a victory. The gods have beaten the demons, and they celebrate: this win is ours, this greatness is ours. But the power behind it was Brahman's, the one reality in everything. So Brahman appears as a strange, wonderful being the gods can't place. They send Agni, god of fire, to find out. Who are you? it asks. I'm Agni, he says. I can burn anything on earth. It sets down one blade of grass. Burn this.
screen: `THE GODS WIN A WAR.` → `'THIS VICTORY IS OURS.'` → `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.`

segments.voice: Agni rushes at it with all his speed, and the grass doesn't even singe. Then Vayu, the wind: I can carry off anything on earth. He can't stir the blade. Then Indra, king of the gods, goes himself, and the being vanishes. In its place stands a radiant woman, Uma, daughter of the mountains. She tells him: that was Brahman. The victory was Brahman's, and you were taking it as yours. The Upanishad's opening names what's underneath: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the eye of the eye. Not what you see; what you see by. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.6. Asmita, I-ness, from asmi, I am, is when the seer and the power of seeing seem to be one self. Drig, the seer. Darshana shakti, the power of seeing, here the mind. And one small, crucial word: iva, as if. They only seem to be one. That's Agni's mistake in a single line: the fire took the power moving through it as its own. Asmita isn't arrogance; a shy person has as much as a loud one. It's the glue that sticks awareness to the body, the moods, the story of me. The Upanishads call the seer the atman, and this is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: you are the one who sees, not the instrument. It's one reason many Hindu families, after a win, say first: by God's grace. Today it's the grade, the goal, the post that soars or flops, and it feels like the whole of who you are. Remember the blade of grass. Notice the one who's looking.

segments.voice: Say silently, I am, and notice what comes with it: a feeling in the chest, a picture of your face, a name, a role. Then notice that you are aware of all of it, and gently ask whether the one who sees is one more thing on the list. You don't need an answer; let the question loosen the glue a little.
I-ness. Asmita, sutra 2.6: the seer and the mind it sees through seem to be one self. Seem, as if, iva, is the key.

segments.voice: Your line: asmita, the seer mistaken for what it sees. Remember the blade of grass. See you tomorrow.

451.title: Bharata and the deer
451.hook: a king who gave up a kingdom is undone by love for a fawn: raga and dvesha, the pull and the push
451.carry: raga and dvesha: the pull and the push
451.tomorrow: a king is told he has seven days to live. how does he spend them?
451.howItsDone: Bharata's story, from the fifth book of the Bhagavata Purana, is often told as a caution about attachment. Some Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages ask students to watch raga and dvesha in daily life, pausing before acting on a like or dislike, and the Bhagavad Gita also names them as obstacles on the path.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Agni and the blade of grass, and I-ness, asmita: the seer mistaken for what it sees. Today, what that sense of me starts doing.
screen: `ASMITA: THE SEER MISTAKEN FOR WHAT IT SEES.`

segments.voice: King Bharata has done what kings almost never do. He's handed his kingdom to his sons and gone to live by a river as a hermit, to worship and meditate. One morning a pregnant doe comes to drink. A lion roars nearby. She leaps the river in terror, her fawn drops into the water, and she dies on the far bank. The newborn is drowning. Bharata wades in and saves it. That's kindness, and the Bhagavata Purana says so. Then he starts raising it.
screen: `A KING TURNED HERMIT.` → `A FAWN FALLS INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE SAVES IT. THEN HE KEEPS IT.`

segments.voice: He feeds the fawn, plays with it, panics when it wanders off. His prayers get shorter; his thoughts of the deer get longer. The man who let go of a kingdom can't let go of one small animal. When Bharata dies, the deer is beside him, and his last thought is the deer. The story says he's born next as a deer, still remembering who he was. The Gita teaches the same: what you think of at the end, you go to. Now Patanjali names what caught him. Sutra 2.7: attraction follows pleasure. Sutra 2.8: aversion follows pain. Raga and dvesha. The key word is anushayi, resting upon: each rests on a memory. Vyasa puts it plainly: raga is the thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure; dvesha, the resentment of pain in one who remembers pain. In these sutras love isn't the problem, and neither is pleasure. Saving the fawn was right. The affliction is the grip that grows, until a memory decides for you. And the two are partners: the deer's sweetness made every absence frightening. The Gita names them as a pair: raga and dvesha sit in the senses; don't fall under their sway. Today it's the person, the show, the phone you reach for before you've chosen to. Love it. Just notice when the pull has taken the wheel.
screen: `A FAWN SAVED. A HEART CAUGHT.` · `HIS LAST THOUGHT: THE DEER.` · `RAGA FOLLOWS PLEASURE. DVESHA FOLLOWS PAIN.` · `RESTING ON MEMORY.` · then, large: `THE GRIP, NOT THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Watch for tiny pulls and pushes as you sit: an itch you want to scratch, a thought of something nice later, a sound you wish would stop. Name each one gently, raga or dvesha, and wait one breath before doing anything. If you pray, try it during your prayer and notice where the mind wanders off to. Often the pull fades by itself.
Anushayi, following after, resting upon. Raga, attraction, follows the memory of pleasure; dvesha, aversion, follows the memory of pain: grooves that pull and push the mind.

segments.voice: Your line: raga and dvesha, the pull and the push. Bharata's love was good; the grip was the trouble. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Parikshit's seven days
452.hook: a king told he has seven days to live spends them listening: the fear of death runs even in the wise
452.carry: abhinivesha: even the wise cling to life
452.tomorrow: an arrow shot in the dark. when does it land?
452.howItsDone: Many Hindu communities hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day recitation of the Bhagavata Purana that remembers the seven days Parikshit listened to Shuka. Near the end of life, families often read scripture and repeat God's name beside the dying person. Students of the Yoga Sutras study abhinivesha with the classical commentary.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata and the deer, and your line, raga and dvesha, the pull and the push. Today, the last of the five afflictions.
screen: `RAGA, DVESHA — THE PULL AND THE PUSH.`

segments.voice: King Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, is out hunting, tired and thirsty. He finds a sage sitting in deep meditation who doesn't answer him. In a flash of anger, the king hangs a dead snake around the sage's shoulders and leaves. The sage's young son hears of it and curses him: in seven days, the serpent Takshaka will bite him, and he will die. Parikshit doesn't fight the curse. He gives his kingdom to his son and sits down on the bank of the Ganga.
screen: `A DEAD SNAKE ON A SAGE.` → `SEVEN DAYS TO LIVE.` → `THE KING SITS BY THE GANGA.`

segments.voice: Sages gather. Parikshit asks them one question: what should a person do who is about to die? Then the young sage Shuka arrives, and for seven days he tells the king the Bhagavata Purana, story after story of God, while the king fasts and listens. Near the end, Shuka tells him, in effect: let go of the thought, I am going to die. That's a creature's thinking. Unlike the body, you weren't born, and you won't be destroyed. This is why many Hindus still hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day reading of the whole text, and why families read scripture and say God's name beside someone near the end. Now Patanjali. Sutra 2.9 names the fifth affliction: abhinivesha, clinging to life. It is svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill, and established even in the wise. Vidushah api. The classical commentary hears in every creature the same wish: may I not stop being. Even a just-hatched worm shrinks from danger. Notice who Parikshit is: a good king, saved by Krishna before he was born. Wisdom alone doesn't empty the fear, and Patanjali doesn't shame anyone for it; he says the afflictions are undone by tracing them back to their source, and quieted by meditation. Parikshit spent his last days on what doesn't die. Day to day, abhinivesha is rarely about dying. It's the grip on how things were: a house, a role, any small ending. The same grab.
screen: `ONE QUESTION, SEVEN DAYS OF STORIES.` · `LET GO OF 'I AM GOING TO DIE.'` · `2.9: CLINGING, BY ITS OWN MOMENTUM.` · `EVEN IN THE WISE.` · then, large: `THE SAME GRAB, IN SMALL ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath run on its own. On each out-breath, say a name silently: Ram, or Krishna, or Om, whichever name you love; if you don't pray, a word like peace. Notice the little pause at the end of the out-breath, and whether something in you hurries to grab the next one. No need to hold it; let each breath come by itself. If anything feels uncomfortable, breathe normally.
Svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill. Abhinivesha, the clinging to going on, runs by itself this way, and stays even in the wise.

segments.voice: Your line: abhinivesha, even the wise cling to life. Parikshit spent his seven days on what doesn't die. Go gently; see you tomorrow.

453.title: Dasharatha's arrow
453.hook: a young prince shoots at a sound in the dark, and the deed ripens decades later: karma, the storehouse of action
453.carry: karma: every deed is a seed that ripens
453.tomorrow: a king gets a thousand years of youth. is it enough?
453.howItsDone: Dasharatha's memory of the boy at the river, from the Ramayana, is one of the best-known Hindu tellings of a deed's fruit returning; later tellings name the boy Shravan Kumar and honor his care for his blind parents. Teachers of the Yoga Sutras present practice as the way to weaken the afflictions that make stored action sprout.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Parikshit's seven days, and abhinivesha: even the wise cling to life, a clinging that flows by its own momentum. Today, what the afflictions do over time.
screen: `ABHINIVESHA: EVEN THE WISE CLING TO LIFE.`

segments.voice: Long before Rama is born, his father Dasharatha is a young prince with a famous skill: he can hit a target by sound alone. One night by the Sarayu river he hears a gurgling at the water's edge. An elephant drinking, he thinks, and he shoots. A cry comes back, a human cry. He runs down and finds a young ascetic, his water pot in the river, an arrow in his side. The boy's parents are old and blind, waiting for that water.
screen: `A SHOT AT A SOUND IN THE DARK.` → `A HUMAN CRY.` → `TWO BLIND PARENTS, WAITING.`

segments.voice: The boy, whom later tellings call Shravan, asks the prince to go to his father, and dies. Dasharatha carries the water to the old couple and confesses. The father, in his grief, says: you too will die grieving for a son. Decades pass. Dasharatha becomes a great king. Then Rama is sent into exile, and on the night Dasharatha dies of that grief, the Ramayana has him remember the river and tell his queen: whatever a person does, good or bad, the doer reaps its fruit. That is karma, one of Hinduism's central teachings. Patanjali gives its workings. Sutra 2.12: karmashaya, the storehouse of action. Every deed leaves a deposit, rooted in the afflictions, lived out in this birth or one unseen. Sutra 2.13: while that root is there, it ripens three ways, as a birth, a life span and what is lived through. And 2.14: joy from merit, pain from its opposite. There's no scorekeeper in the sutras. It's closer to farming: seed, soil, time. The commentary adds hope: rice in its husk can sprout, but husked or roasted, it won't. The afflictions are the husk; thin them by practice and old seeds lose their power. And notice who names Dasharatha's deed: Dasharatha. Many teachers say karma is for reading your own actions, not for judging someone else's pain. Today the storehouse fills quietly: the sharp text, the patient answer, the help nobody saw. Each one a seed.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you did yesterday, kind or unkind, and notice what it left in you: a warmth, a tightness, a replay. That's the deposit; just see it clearly, the way you'd hold a seed in your palm, without judging or fixing it. Then set it down and come back to the breath, which is happening now, not yesterday.
Karmashaya, the storehouse of action. Every deed leaves a deposit there, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and an experience.

454.title: Yayati's thousand years
454.hook: a king borrows his son's youth for a thousand years and learns why, to the discerning, even pleasure holds pain
454.carry: duhkha: feeding desire never puts it out
454.tomorrow: a born hermit is sent to learn freedom from a king. why a king?
454.howItsDone: Yayati's verse about fire and ghee is quoted across Hindu texts, including the Bhagavata Purana and the Manusmriti. Many Hindus keep fasts such as Ekadashi as devotion and as practice in going without, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline: the illness and its cause, with the cure and remedy to follow.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's arrow, karmashaya, and your line: karma, every deed is a seed that ripens. Today, a line that sounds gloomy at first.
screen: `KARMA — EVERY DEED A SEED.`

segments.voice: King Yayati is cursed with sudden old age. His father-in-law, the sage Shukra, leaves one way out: if a son will take the old age, Yayati can have that son's youth. Four sons refuse. The youngest, Puru, says yes. So Yayati is young again, and the Mahabharata says he enjoys it for a thousand years. Every pleasure a king could want. At the end of it, he calls Puru back.
screen: `A CURSE OF OLD AGE.` → `A SON GIVES HIS YOUTH.` → `A THOUSAND YEARS OF PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: He gives the youth back, and says the line Hindus still quote: desire is never quenched by enjoying what's desired. Like fire fed with ghee, it only grows. Then he goes to the forest. A thousand years, and it wasn't enough, because enough was never coming. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.15: to the discerning, all is duhkha, suffering. It sounds gloomy. It's a diagnosis, and Yayati is the case. Patanjali gives four reasons even pleasure hides pain. Change: the sweet thing is already ending, like borrowed youth. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it. Impressions: each pleasure leaves a groove that wants more, the ghee on the fire. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other. The commentary says most people are like an arm: a thread of wool lands and nothing is felt. The discerning are like the eye, and the same thread hurts. Then the turn, 2.16: heyam duhkham anagatam, the suffering not yet come is to be avoided. And 2.17 names the cause: the seer joined to the seen. Hindus who fast, on Ekadashi, in Navratri, on a weekday for a chosen god, do it first as devotion; many teachers add Yayati's reason: going without a little, on purpose, keeps the fire from growing. Today it's the next order, the next episode, the next scroll. Yayati already ran that experiment, for a thousand years.
screen: `FIRE FED WITH GHEE ONLY GROWS.` · `2.15: TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING.` · `FOUR WAYS PLEASURE HIDES PAIN.` · `AVOID THE PAIN NOT YET COME.` · then, large: `FEEDING DESIRE NEVER PUTS IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want that keeps coming back, a snack, a scroll, one more episode. Feel it rise, like a flame. This once, don't feed it. Watch what the flame does when no ghee comes: it flares, then often settles. If you pray, offer that want to God the way a fasting family offers the day. If you don't, just let it be a small, chosen going-without.
Duhkha, suffering, pain, unease, the opposite of sukha, ease. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.
screen: `DUHKHA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: duhkha, feeding desire never puts it out. Yayati took a thousand years to learn it. Until tomorrow.

455.title: Janaka, the king who was free
455.hook: a born hermit is sent to learn freedom from a king in a palace: the world is for experience and liberation
455.carry: bhoga and apavarga: the world is for both
455.tomorrow: two students look into the water for the self. only one goes back.
455.howItsDone: Hindu teaching names four aims of life, dharma, artha, kama and moksha, and Janaka of Mithila is the classic example of a householder king who was free. In the Samkhya and Yoga schools, nature is understood to exist for the sake of awareness, offering both experience and the chance of liberation; students study these sutras with the classical commentary.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yayati's thousand years, and your line, duhkha, feeding desire never puts it out, with its cause, the seer and the seen tangled. Today ends the week.
screen: `DUHKHA — FIRE FED WITH GHEE.`

segments.voice: Shuka, the young sage who sat beside the dying Parikshit, wanted nothing from the world, the stories say, almost from birth. His father, Vyasa, sends him to learn about freedom anyway, and not from a hermit. From a king. In the Mahabharata, Shuka walks to Mithila, to King Janaka. The guards make him wait at the gate. He doesn't mind. Then he's led inside, into gardens, music and every comfort, and none of it moves him.
screen: `A HERMIT SENT TO A KING.` → `HE WAITS AT THE GATE.` → `A PALACE, AND HE'S UNMOVED.`

segments.voice: And then Janaka, a man with a kingdom to run, teaches him. Janaka is remembered in the Mahabharata for one line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. In the Gita, Krishna names him: Janaka and others reached perfection through action. A king, ruling, and free. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.18. The seen, everything that can be watched, the mountains, the body, the mind itself, is made of light, activity and stillness, and it has a purpose: bhoga and apavarga. Experience and liberation. The world is there so the seer can taste it, and so the seer can be free of the confusion. Both, not one instead of the other. Sutra 2.21: the seen exists for the seer's sake. And 2.22 adds something tender: when one person is free, the world doesn't vanish. It stays, shared with everyone still living in it. Janaka didn't walk away from his people; he kept ruling them. Hindu teaching makes room for this. It names four aims of life side by side: dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation. Not the world or freedom. Both. So, the week. The passing taken for lasting. The power taken as mine. The pull and the push. The clinging, even in the wise. Seeds that ripen. Fire fed with ghee. And today, the turn: the same world that tangles you is the way through.
screen: `IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.` · `2.18: THE SEEN HAS A PURPOSE.` · `EXPERIENCE AND LIBERATION.` · `2.22: IT STAYS FOR EVERYONE ELSE.` · `FOUR AIMS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `THE WORLD IS FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: First, experience: let one sense fill up, the sounds in the room or the light through your eyelids, and taste it fully without grabbing. Then freedom: notice that the sound comes and goes, and the hearing stays. Move between the two, tasting and watching, as many times as you like.
Apavarga, release, liberation. In the Yoga Sutras, the seen exists for the seer, for two things: experience and liberation.

segments.voice: Your line: bhoga and apavarga, the world is for both: living and freedom. Janaka had a palace and was free. That's the week, day four hundred fifty-five.
